newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: French demands set EMU on uncharted path.
newsitem.headline: French demands set EMU on uncharted path.

text.p: France's demand to reconsider a budget stability pact for those joining economic and monetary union (EMU) has put Europe's planned single currency on an uncharted course from which there is no clear exit.

EU diplomats on Monday offered a mix of caution, guarded optimism and frustration to the new French government's request for additional time to review an accord which many believed was virtually a done deal.

The French position, understandable to some extent given the Socialist government's short time in office, has even raised doubts over agreement on several broader EU issues which were due to be ratified at an Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.
"The real question is whether there is a link between France's demands and the IGC (inter-governmental conference)," said one EU diplomat.
"The problem is nobody knows about the content of what they really want," he added.
What is clear, say diplomats, is that Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's new government believes it has an obligation to the voters which swept it into office.
Jobs are their number one concern and it is that which the government wants addressed in any agreement on budgetary discipline inside EMU.

The problem for the EU, however, is how to maintain confidence in the single currency while at the same time accommodating the demands of one of Europe's most important economies, one that is indispensable to monetary union.

"There were a fair number of people who wanted to avoid the impression of a setback," said another EU official, who was unclear about what contingency plans might be developed if the budget pact was not approved in Amsterdam.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel was said to be worried about reaction in the financial markets.
There were also rumblings that the French would want to hold up agreement on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism for the euro as well as its legal framework if their concerns were not met.

Should talks on the stability pact extend beyond next week's summit, diplomats say the options open to the EU included holding a special summit shortly afterwards rather than waiting until the next planned summit in Luxembourg in December.

It was acknowledged that playing a waiting-game could risk further undermining investor confidence, already at a premium in financial markets given the leftward political shift in France and Germany's ongoing budget problems. Ultimately, what happens to the euro's timetable hinges on what France actually wants and how acceptable it is to its European partners.
But to the extent that Monday's meeting revisited the many issues which were already negotiated and then renegotiated several times over, the results were certainly disappointing.
"It's clear this puts the whole thing into limbo," said another EU diplomat.
"We are now talking about the same things we discussed a year ago. Where this is headed, I don't know," he added.
